correctness.rationale: Here m=a+b is a unit modulo p, so s exists, q-1=mw>0, w is a p-adic unit, and bw is -1 modulo p. The base-q products mn and an have respectively digits epsilon_j(q-1) and epsilon_j aw, all in [0,q-1], with no cross-block carry. Within every occupied block the top base-p digits are all p-1, so every Lucas factor is a unit; unoccupied blocks are zero on both sides. Since epsilon_0=1, p divides bn+1 and does not divide the binomial. The digit strings of n itself have digits 0 or w, so they are distinct and strictly below q^r. At r=floor(log_q X) this gives the exact stated lower bound, at least X^delta/4. The p-adic witness closure consists exactly of the infinite choices by compactness of binary sequence space and density of finite truncations. Two choices first differing at j have distance p^(-sj); the length-r cylinders are intersections with residue-class balls of radius q^(-r). Cover by the 2^(r-1) cylinders for the dimension upper bound. Their uniform Bernoulli masses are 2^(1-r); for arbitrary small radii between successive q-powers the same cylinder bound gives a constant times radius^delta, proving the reverse bound by mass distribution.
residual_risks: The exponent is a lower-bound exponent for the exception count. The dimension is exact only for the constructed closure, not for all failures. Cylinders are balls in the subspace metric, not entire ambient Z_p balls.

No credit is assigned for Lucas's theorem or general path-set dimension theory.

value.rationale: The result strengthens a natural qualitative infinitude theorem by replacing isolated witnesses with a uniformly described power-law family, introducing a positive-dimensional geometric substructure. Even a nonoptimal exponent quantifies how often the failures can be guaranteed under the original hypothesis, which the earlier prime-power sequence does not achieve.
residual_risks: No density, optimal exponent, or exact dimension of the complete failure set follows.
